description:
We are Space Archeology, a team of undergraduate students majoring in Management. We are participating in the NASA Hackathon to challenge ourselves, bring creative ideas to life, and gain new experience.

We are creative, ambitious, open-minded, and team-oriented. We are looking for like-minded people who are passionate about space, technology, and innovation, have skills in programming, design, or data analysis, or are simply eager to share ideas and learn new things.
summary: Legends of Stardust is an interactive digital comic for kids aged 6–10 about NASA's abandoned hardware on the Moon and Mars. By turning "cold metal" into living heroes and engaging mini-quests, it makes real space science fun and removes the fear of STEM. Since ages 6–10 are critical for shaping lifelong curiosity, this project rescues historic space missions from dusty archives, making science emotionally relatable while building critical thinking skills and inspiring the next generation of engineers and explorers.
details:
• What the project does and how it works:Legends of Stardust is an interactive digital comic-game for kids aged 6–10 about real historic NASA space spacecraft (such as the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle and rovers Opportunity and Sojourner) that permanently remain on the surface of the Moon and Mars. The project is built as a non-linear digital story with interactive panels and micro-quests. Readers choose a mission, meet the robots from a first-person perspective, and help them overcome real challenges through simple interactive tasks.
  • What advantages it has: The project features a zero-barrier entry thanks to its familiar comic format. By exporting as an interactive PDF with internal links (via Canva), the book runs on any device without requiring additional software installation. Technical objects are presented as emotional pioneer characters, evoking genuine empathy and interest in children.
  • What the expected impact of the project is: The project bridges the gap between complex science and children's perception, removing the fear of STEM disciplines through play. Since ages 6–10 are critical for shaping lifelong curiosity, transforming abandoned space heritage into inspiration fosters critical thinking and prepares the next generation of explorers and future engineers (the Artemis Generation).
  • What tools and software were used: The project utilized Canva for slide design and layouts. Google Translate was used where necessary for language adaptation and terminology checks, while artificial intelligence tools generated the visual style. Open NASA archive resources (official artifact catalogs, mission timelines, and image libraries) served as the scientific foundation.
  • How creative the project is: The project is highly visual and innovative in form. It combines gamification (mini-quests, path choices, interactive tasks like the "Mars rock detective") with child psychology, creating a complete interactive story where the exploration machines themselves act as the main characters.
  • What factors your team considered: The team adapted text complexity, sentence length, and material presentation to match the cognitive abilities of children aged 6–10. All historical and technical details (instrument operations and mission circumstances) are strictly based on real NASA archival data, and technical implementation is optimized for stable performance across any device.
